Your remit is the specific area of work, responsibility, or authority that has been officially assigned to you — and just as importantly, it defines the limits of that responsibility. It tells you what you are and are not supposed to deal with.

Think of it like a job description, but more focused on boundaries than duties. It answers the question: "What is this person or group officially in charge of?"

Two things are almost always true when the word "remit" is used as a noun:

1. The responsibility was given by someone else.
You don't just decide your own remit. A manager, organisation, government, or some authority assigns it to you. This is why "remit" carries a sense of official delegation — someone handed you this area of responsibility.

2. It has edges.
This is crucial. A remit is not unlimited. It has a boundary. Something either falls within your remit (it's your territory) or falls outside your remit (it's not your problem to solve — someone else handles that).

"The police officer said that investigating financial fraud was not within his remit — that was a matter for a specialist unit."

Here, his remit is general policing. Financial fraud sits outside that boundary.

"The new committee has a broad remit to improve healthcare across the country."

Here, a wide area of responsibility has been assigned to the committee. The word "broad" tells us the remit is large and covers many things.

"As a customer service agent, fixing bugs in the software is outside my remit. I can log the issue, but the developers need to fix it."

The agent's remit is helping customers. Fixing code belongs to a different person's remit.

"The inspector's remit was specifically limited to reviewing safety procedures, nothing else."

Notice the limits being spelled out clearly — that's very typical of how "remit" is used.
The Word Does a Very Specific Job

"Remit" as a noun is not just a fancy word for "job" or "task." It is specifically about scope and authority — what falls under your responsibility versus what doesn't. This makes it especially useful in professional, organisational, and governmental settings, where it matters deeply who is responsible for what.

Compare:

  • A task is a single thing you need to do.
  • A job is your overall role.
  • A remit is the defined territory of responsibility within which you operate.
The Most Important Phrases to Know

These are the fixed, natural phrases you'll encounter constantly with this word:

PhraseWhat it means
within someone's remitIt is their area of responsibility
outside someone's remitIt is not their responsibility
fall within/outside a remitSomething belongs (or doesn't belong) to an area of responsibility
have a remit to do somethingBe officially authorised/assigned to do something
a broad/narrow remitA wide-ranging vs. tightly focused area of responsibility

(Example: "The agency has a remit to regulate online content.")

"Remit" as a noun is used heavily in British English — in government, law, business, and academia. You'll encounter it constantly in news articles, official reports, and workplace conversations in the UK. It is used less frequently in American English, where people are more likely to say "mandate," "scope," or "jurisdiction" to convey the same idea.
One-Line Summary to Lock It In

Remit (noun) = the officially assigned area of responsibility and authority given to a person or group, including its limits — what they are and are not supposed to handle.

If you ever see it in a sentence and feel uncertain, ask yourself: "Whose job is it to deal with this, and up to what point?" — that's exactly what "remit" is answering.
